name: Hesperidin
lead: Hesperidin is a flavanone glycoside found in citrus fruits, concentrated in the white inner peel; its aglycone is hesperetin.[1] It was first isolated in 1828 by the French chemist M. Lebreton.[1] It is sold as a dietary supplement, often combined with diosmin or vitamin C, in products aimed at venous and capillary complaints.[2][17]

In appearance communities it is discussed in the context of puffiness and dark circles, based on the idea that it supports small blood vessels. The sources reviewed contain no trial of hesperidin for periorbital puffiness or dark circles; the clinical literature concerns venous, metabolic and other conditions, and Wikipedia describes research on hesperidin as preliminary, with reviews finding no clear effect on blood lipids or blood pressure and inconclusive results on endothelial function.[1]

paras: Hesperidin and related citrus flavonoids are used in supplements for chronic venous insufficiency, haemorrhoids and capillary fragility, often in combination with diosmin.[2] A US over-the-counter label for a bruising product lists hesperidin methyl chalcone among citrus bioflavonoid ingredients alongside vitamin C, zinc, arnica and bromelain.[18] Its use for facial puffiness or under-eye circles is promoted in some products and discussions but has not been tested in published trials found in the sources reviewed.

Laboratory and animal work describes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity for hesperidin and hesperetin, including activation of the Nrf2 pathway.[19][20] Authors have proposed effects on capillary permeability and endothelial function, but human evidence is limited.[1][20]

Hesperidin is poorly soluble and is largely absorbed as hesperetin after gut bacteria remove the sugar moiety. Human bioavailability of hesperidin and the related flavanone narirutin has been measured after orange juice ingestion.[21] A registered study compared the bioavailability of three hesperidin extracts.[22]

Reviews note no signs of toxicity at normal intakes of hesperidin and related compounds.[20] Mild gastrointestinal effects, headache and rash are occasionally reported with supplements in general; trials in the sources reviewed did not focus on adverse effects.
No studies found on hesperidin for facial puffiness, dark circles or other cosmetic outcomes.

Related research in other conditions: a 12-week open-label randomized trial in 98 people with metabolic syndrome compared hesperidin, flaxseed and their combination;[8] a controlled trial examined sulodexide and phlebotonic drugs in venous ulcers;[10] older European trials examined micronised flavonoid fractions in venous disease and in upper-limb lymphoedema after breast cancer treatment.[11][12] Systematic reviews of polyphenols include hesperidin among agents studied in rheumatoid arthritis.[5] A review of citrus flavonoids describes much of the evidence as epidemiological or preclinical.[17] Registered trials examine hesperidin for cognition, bone health in postmenopausal women, COVID-19 symptoms and metabolic syndrome.[23][24][25][26]

timeline.event: Hesperidin first isolated from citrus peel by M. Lebreton.[1]
